USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariff schedule in place as leverage and continue the Washington round with Liu He without new hikes or rollbacks. Press for a written, enforceable package on IP, forced tech transfer, and a snap-back mechanism; treat Chinese purchase offers as a down payment, not the deal. If talks remain productive into the March 1 window, hold List 3 at 10% rather than automatically lifting it to 25%—do not trade away tariffs for a handshake.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a modest US opportunity, not a high-danger moment. The G20 truce (2018-12-01) froze the List 3 hike and opened a 90-day window; subsequent rounds (2019-01-07, 2019-01-30, 2019-02-14) show purchase progress while enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues remain open—exactly the 301 case that started this (2018-03-22). That is leverage, not distress: China’s SA merchandise exports are down ~8.7% in the window and Beijing has resumed soybean buying and dangled larger purchases, while US VIX has fallen back to 14.02 (2019-02-20) from the December spike. Offsetting costs are real but contained—US goods exports to China are down ~17% (EXPCH), industrial production has slipped to 102.8, and Michigan sentiment dipped to 91.2 in January before a partial rebound to 93.8—so this is not a +0.5 GDP-drag reading. Escalating List 3 to 25% now, while Trump has already said March 1 “is not a magical date” and Mnuchin called Beijing talks “productive,” would risk collapsing a live negotiation and inviting broader retaliation against farm-belt goods. Conceding or rolling back would repeat the May 2018 false truce (2018-05-19/05-29): purchases without an enforcement mechanism. Huawei/Meng charges (2019-01-28) and the Kovrig/Spavor detentions sit on a parallel legal/consular track; they raise atmosphere risk but the White House has kept them formally separate from the trade table, so they do not justify either a hostage-style concession or a tariff blow-up this week.
key_factors: Live high-level talks with purchase progress but no enforcement/IP deal
Existing ~$250B Section 301 coverage is the main US lever; March 1 List 3 hike is optional not mandatory
China export softening and resumed ag purchases show opponent under more pressure than the US
US farm-export and sentiment costs are real but not recessionary
Huawei/Meng legal track is formally separate; do not bargain it into a trade concession

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
Another round of talks (through Feb 15). Progress reported on purchases; enforcement mechanism still disputed.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
USTR Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
US exports to China latest 8083.6 (2019-02) vs 9733.1 (2018-09), about -17% in the window.
China merchandise exports latest 197.6B (2019-02) vs 216.3B (2018-09), about -8.7%.
VIX 14.02 on 2019-02-20 after December spike above 36; market stress has receded during the truce.
Michigan sentiment 91.2 in Jan 2019 then 93.8 in Feb, down from 100.1 in Sep 2018—softening, not collapse.
Talks continue in Washington; Trump said March 1 'is not a magical date' and the real question is whether to raise tariffs.
Mnuchin called Beijing talks productive; White House said much work remains on structural issues; Trump said he might extend if close.
